Title: Effect of liraglutide on depressive symptoms in overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes: protocol for a pilot randomized controlled trial
Snippet: Introduction Patients with concurrent obesity, type 2 diabetes, and depression experience high disease severity and prevalence. This triad of conditions compromises quality of life and treatment adherence, further exacerbating disease progression. Therapeutic strategies for such patients must address both glycemic control and psychological well-being. Liraglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), offers benefits beyond glucose-lowering and weight reduction, with emerging evidence suggesting it may also alleviate depressive symptoms. Therefore, liraglutide represents a promising intervention for managing depression in patients with obesity and diabetes. Objectives This study aims to assess the therapeutic efficacy of liraglutide in overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes and comorbid depression, with a specific focus on its antidepressant effects. Methods This is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial. Sixty eligible participants will be randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either liraglutide (initiated at 0.6 mg/day, titrated weekly to a maximum of 1.8 mg/day) or a matched placebo, as an adjunct to standard care for 12 weeks. The primary endpoints include blood glucose levels, glycated hemoglobin, body mass index, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale score, and metrics derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (resting-state fMRI). Secondary endpoints will assess changes in inflammatory biomarkers (tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6), oxidative stress indicators (superoxide dismutase, malondialdehyde), homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance, insulin sensitivity index, and homeostasis model assessment of β-cell function. Conclusions This trial will provide preliminary data on the effects of liraglutide on depressive symptoms in overweight/obese patients with type 2 diabetes. The findings are expected to provide a basis and reference for subsequent large-scale clinical research.
</snippet>

Summary and framing

- Bottom line: Current clinical evidence does not establish that GLP‑1 receptor agonists (GLP‑1 RAs) are effective antidepressants for major depressive disorder (MDD) as a primary psychiatric diagnosis; small open‑label signals of benefit exist, but randomized trials generally do not show superior antidepressant efficacy versus controls, and the literature is contradictory with reports of mood worsening or suicidality in rare cases.<cite id="4f61a454-1">Current clinical evidence regarding the impact of GLP‑1 analogs on depressive symptoms remains contradictory, with some trials supporting effectiveness while others report contrary findings, including exacerbation of mood disturbances and rare suicide attempts</cite><cite id="9fe6e97a-1">Liraglutide produced significant reductions in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores in a 4‑week open‑label study in patients with MDD or bipolar disorder with impaired executive function, but failed to show a significant antidepressant effect in a randomized controlled trial</cite><cite id="9fe6e97a-3">Across small studies, GLP‑1 RAs may be useful for depressive disorders but reliable clinical reports are few; more studies are needed to determine whether GLP‑1 agonists can serve as supportive therapy or benefit treatment‑resistant depression</cite>. Reviews and protocols consistently call for adequately powered randomized trials in patients with MDD, not only comorbid diabetes or obesity.<cite id="4f61a454-1">A multicenter, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled RCT with ≥700 patients and dual HAM‑D and HbA1c endpoints over ≥12 months is warranted in patients with comorbid depressive disorder and diabetes; dose–response and comparative evaluations are lacking</cite><cite id="4f61a454-2">Reviews note many reports on depression outcomes in GLP‑1 RA literature but emphasize the need for rigorous designs and standardized depression endpoints</cite>.

What GLP‑1 RAs are and why depression-specific questions matter

- GLP‑1 RAs are incretin mimetics approved for diabetes and obesity that cross the blood–brain barrier, act on central GLP‑1 receptors, and modulate appetite, energy expenditure, and glycemia; their potential antidepressant effects are hypothesized to arise from effects on neuroinflammation, neurogenesis, neurotrophic signaling, and neurotransmission.<cite id="4f61a454-3">Semaglutide crosses the blood–brain barrier and exhibits neuroprotective properties; preliminary data suggest antidepressant effects via modulation of neuroinflammation and hippocampal plasticity</cite><cite id="4f61a454-3">GLP‑1 is released from intestinal L‑cells and neurons in the nucleus tractus solitarius, and its central actions are implicated in multiple systemic and psychiatric effects</cite>. However, regulatory labeling has focused on glycemia and weight, and depression is not a primary indication; thus, effectiveness for primary MDD remains unproven.<cite id="9fe6e97a-3">Evidence that GLP‑1 RAs are useful for depressive disorders exists, but the number of reliable clinical reports is very low, and their approval and use are primarily centered on metabolic indications</cite>.

Clinical trial evidence specifically in depression or MDD

- Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) testing GLP‑1 RAs as antidepressants are few, heterogeneous, and typically embedded in metabolic disease. In adults with type 2 diabetes, a 26‑week RCT found liraglutide reduced weight and HbA1c but did not significantly reduce Beck Depression Inventory scores versus control, despite improvements in glycemic control.<cite id="9fe6e97a-1">In a randomized controlled trial in adults with T2DM, 26 weeks of liraglutide reduced body weight and HbA1c but failed to reduce BDI scores versus control by a significant amount</cite><cite id="9fe6e97a-3">A pooled analysis of phase 2/3 liraglutide trials for weight management reported no major neuropsychiatric safety concerns, but the same RCTs did not demonstrate significant antidepressant efficacy</cite>. Protocolized pilot RCTs have been designed to test liraglutide’s antidepressant effects in comorbid diabetes/obesity, but preliminary results are awaited and underscore the need for adequately powered trials.<cite id="9fe6e97a-0">A randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled pilot trial (n=60) tested liraglutide versus placebo for 12 weeks with HAM‑D as a primary endpoint in overweight/obese patients with T2D and comorbid depression</cite><cite id="9fe6e97a-2">Given meta‑analyses suggesting improvement in depression scale scores in diabetes but with some studies showing mood fluctuations, a pilot RCT protocol emphasizes the need for rigorous trials to resolve inconsistencies</cite>.

- In semaglutide trials for weight management, patients with moderate/severe depression (PHQ‑9 ≥15) were excluded, limiting generalizability to primary MDD and obscuring efficacy in clinically significant depression. Subgroup analyses suggest comparable weight‑loss efficacy regardless of antidepressant use and largely consistent adverse event profiles, but they do not establish antidepressant efficacy and highlight the need for dedicated psychiatric trials.<cite id="9d5022c4-3">Semaglutide trials excluded patients with PHQ‑9 ≥15 and those with a history of suicide attempt or current suicidal ideation, limiting generalizability to people with more severe depression</cite><cite id="9d5022c4-3">Across STEP 1–3 and 5 trials, semaglutide showed weight‑loss efficacy comparable to non‑antidepressant users with a safety profile consistent with the GLP‑1 class, but efficacy and psychiatric safety with concurrent antidepressants require further study</cite>.

- Outside RCTs, small open‑label and cohort studies provide mixed signals: some report reductions on depression scales with liraglutide or exenatide in comorbid T2D/obesity, while others find no change in depression risk or outcomes, underscoring inconsistency and limited power.<cite id="4f61a454-2">A nonrandomized trial of exenatide reported reductions in depression scale scores in patients with T2D, and a cohort of 1,735 patients starting incretin therapies showed significant reduction in depressive symptoms versus control</cite><cite id="4f61a454-2">In young women with PCOS and obesity treated with liraglutide, quality‑of‑life improved but no differences in depression risk were found</cite><cite id="9fe6e97a-1">An open‑label study in 19 subjects with MDD or bipolar disorder reported significant HDRS reductions with liraglutide, while an RCT showed no significant effect on depression symptoms</cite>. Narrative reviews also cite improvements in health‑related quality of life with semaglutide (e.g., SUSTAIN 6), without depression as a primary endpoint, complicating interpretation.<cite id="4f61a454-2">Semaglutide improved health‑related quality of life in SUSTAIN 6 over two years, but depressive symptom endpoints were not specifically established</cite>.

Mechanistic rationale and preclinical/translational support

- Multiple mechanistic lines support antidepressant plausibility: central GLP‑1 signaling modulates dopaminergic and neurotrophic pathways (e.g., DRD3, BDNF/CREB), reduces inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL‑6, CRH), and may restore altered lipid and amino‑acid metabolites implicated in depression; these pathways are frequently dysregulated in MDD.<cite id="4f61a454-1">In silico analysis suggests semaglutide interacts with dopaminergic and neurotrophic signaling (DRD3, BDNF, CREB1, CRH, IL‑6, DPP4), pathways implicated in depression</cite><cite id="0bd76137-4">Dulaglutide modulates lipids (sphingolipids, lysophospholipids, phospholipids) and may restore imbalances linked to depressive disorder; it may increase hippocampal N‑acetyl‑L‑aspartic acid and decrease glutamic acid and arginine/proline pathways associated with depressive behaviors</cite>. Preclinical models (chronic mild stress, chronic unpredictable mild stress) show dulaglutide and liraglutide reduce depressive‑like behaviors and improve hippocampal neuroplasticity, aligning with proposed human mechanisms but not constituting clinical proof.<cite id="0bd76137-3">Dulaglutide produced significant antidepressant effects in a chronic mild stress depression model, and liraglutide alleviated depression and anxiety‑like behaviors in mice by improving hippocampal neuroplasticity</cite><cite id="4f61a454-3">Semaglutide’s antidepressant effects in preliminary models are attributed to modulation of neuroinflammation and hippocampal plasticity</cite>.

Safety and tolerability in psychiatric populations

- Psychiatric adverse events have been reported with GLP‑1 RAs, including depressive disorders and suicidal ideation in pharmacovigilance databases; onset is often within weeks, and while rates across agents do not differ statistically, these signals necessitate caution in patients at mood‑disturbance risk.<cite id="9d5022c4-4">Across FAERS/VigiBase reports, median times to onset of depressive disorders were 28 days for liraglutide and 23 days for semaglutide; cumulative occurrence showed no significant differences across GLP‑1 RAs, and “depression suicidal” was classified as random failure</cite>. In liraglutide’s pooled phase 2/3 weight‑management trials, no major neuropsychiatric safety concerns were identified, but earlier clinical trials documented mood disturbances and depressive symptoms in subsets of patients; a case report of liraglutide‑associated depression with suicidality further underscores the risk signal, albeit in an individual case.<cite id="9fe6e97a-3">A pooled analysis of liraglutide trials reported no major neuropsychiatric safety concerns, yet earlier trials documented depressive symptoms and mood disturbances in subsets of patients</cite><cite id="9fe6e97a-4">A case report described liraglutide‑induced depression with suicidality in an obese adult, highlighting potential psychiatric risks alongside established antiobesity benefits</cite>. For semaglutide, subgroup exclusions for severe depression limit risk–benefit characterization in primary MDD; overall adverse events are consistent with the class profile.<cite id="9d5022c4-3">Semaglutide trials excluded patients with moderate to severe depression, and adverse events were consistent with GLP‑1 class, but psychiatric safety in co‑treated MDD remains insufficiently characterized</cite>.

Regulatory/clinical labeling and practice implications

- Liraglutide is approved for diabetes and obesity and has depression listed among possible adverse reactions; evidence does not support depression as a primary indication, and labeling emphasizes weight and glycemic effects. Dulaglutide has been studied for broader cardiometabolic outcomes and is under evaluation for non‑diabetic indications, but depression as a primary endpoint is not established in regulatory approvals.<cite id="9fe6e97a-3">Depression is not currently a primary indication for GLP‑1 RAs; evidence for usefulness in depressive disorders is limited and requires more robust clinical studies</cite><cite id="0bd76137-1">Dulaglutide’s cardiovascular outcomes trial (REWIND) established benefits in T2D populations, illustrating broader regulatory pathways but not depression efficacy</cite>. Clinically, GLP‑1 RAs may be considered as adjunctive therapy or in patients with comorbid obesity/T2D and depressive symptoms, with close monitoring for mood changes; however, guideline‑level recommendations specific to primary MDD are lacking, and large, well‑controlled trials are needed before routine use for primary MDD.<cite id="4f61a454-1">Reviews emphasize contradictory findings and call for head‑to‑head trials and comparative evaluations to determine relative efficacy and safety, including as adjunctive therapy to conventional antidepressants</cite><cite id="4f61a454-2">Narrative reviews synthesize mixed psychiatric outcomes and urge systematic evaluation with standardized depression endpoints and longer follow‑up</cite>.

What evidence would resolve uncertainty

- Positive outcomes would include superiority of a GLP‑1 RA versus an active antidepressant or placebo on validated MDD scales (HAM‑D, MADRS) in 8–12 week RCTs with remission/functional endpoints, plus durability in maintenance trials; negative or neutral results would argue against first‑line use. Comparative head‑to‑head trials, stratified by depression severity and weight/T2D comorbidity, and mechanistic biomarker studies (neuroinflammation, neurotrophic signaling) would clarify effect size, durability, and pathways.<cite id="4f61a454-1">An adequately powered, multicenter, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled RCT in comorbid depressive disorder and diabetes with HAM‑D and HbA1c dual endpoints over ≥12 months is warranted; dose–response and comparative evaluations across agents and populations are needed</cite>. Safety analyses with prespecified suicidality outcomes and bipolar‑switch monitoring would be essential in MDD populations.

Practical answer to the question

- Are GLP‑1 receptor agonists effective for primary MDD? Current evidence does not demonstrate reliable, first‑line antidepressant efficacy for GLP‑1 RAs in primary MDD; small open‑label studies show occasional improvements, but randomized trials generally fail to outperform placebo on depression scales, and contradictory findings with rare mood exacerbations limit confidence. Mechanistic plausibility is strong, and select populations with comorbid metabolic disease may benefit on quality‑of‑life and weight, but depression outcomes remain inconsistent. Consequently, GLP‑1 RAs should not be considered proven standalone therapies for primary MDD at present, and clinicians should weigh limited potential benefits against risks, monitor mood closely, and consider GLP‑1 RAs as adjuncts within comprehensive care until robust RCTs define efficacy in primary MDD.<cite id="9fe6e97a-1">Randomized data show liraglutide failed to reduce depression scores versus control despite glycemic benefits</cite><cite id="9fe6e97a-3">Reliable clinical reports are few and mixed; more trials are needed before recommending GLP‑1 agonists for depressive disorders</cite><cite id="4f61a454-1">Evidence is contradictory with reports of mood worsening or suicidality; RCTs specifically in MDD are needed</cite><cite id="9d5022c4-3">Semaglutide subgroup exclusions for severe depression limit generalizability and underscore the need for dedicated MDD trials</cite><cite id="4f61a454-2">Quality‑of‑life improvements with semaglutide occur without established antidepressant endpoints; mixed psychiatric outcomes across cohorts argue for cautious, adjunctive use</cite>. </answer>

Title: Metabolic Modulators in Depression: Emerging Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities
Snippet: This limitation likely reflects the relatively recent introduction of these therapeutic classes into clinical practice. A multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized controlled trial (n ≥ 700) is warranted in patients with comorbid depressive disorder and diabetes, employing both HAM-D scores and HbA1c levels as dual endpoints over extended follow-up periods (≥12 months). Moreover, there is a lack of studies evaluating the dose-dependent efficacy of these agents in reducing depressive symptoms. Importantly, current clinical evidence regarding the impact of GLP-1 analogs on depressive symptoms remains contradictory. While some trials support their effectiveness in alleviating depressive symptoms, others have reported contrary findings, with indications that GLP-1 analogs may exacerbate mood disturbances and, in rare cases, contribute to suicide attempts. In addition, given that all the reviewed drug classes exhibit antidepressant effects, future research should focus on comparative evaluations or investigate their role as adjunctive therapy to conventional agents to determine their relative efficacy and optimize therapeutic selection. Similarly, no clinical investigations have systematically compared outcomes across more than two patient subgroups, for example, by assessing whether GLP-1 agonists demonstrate equivalent efficacy in individuals with T2DM, obesity, combined T2DM and obesity, or T2DM/obesity with additional comorbidities-despite the likelihood that treatment responses differ across these populations. Furthermore, there is a lack of head-to-head comparisons of individual GLP-1 analogs, even though available clinical data suggest that semaglutide, liraglutide, and dulaglutide may exert differential effects on the alleviation or exacerbation of depressive symptoms. Title: The Impact of Various Methods of Obesity Treatment on the Quality of Life and Mental Health—A Narrative Review
Snippet: Liraglutide, semaglutide, exenatide, and dulaglutide belong to the group of human GLP-1 analogs. They are a new class of glucose-lowering medications whose action on incretin mimetic activation has been approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus, and some of them have also been approved for the treatment of obesity [79,80]. GLP-1 receptors can be found in a variety of body systems, including the central nervous system [81]. In the available medical literature, there are numerous reports on the impact of mental disorders such as depression [81]. Grant, et al, in a not-randomized trial, investigated the influence of exenatide on psychological and quality of life changes in participants diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Treatment with GLP-1 receptor agonists resulted in a reduction in the depression scale [82]. In the cohort study of 1735 patients with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes who had incretin-based therapies, a significant reduction in depressive symptoms was observed compared to the control group [83]. 

Multiple studies prove the beneficial effect of GLP-1 analog therapy on the quality of life measured with various scales. The study conducted by Kahal, et al, in young women with PCOS and obesity treated with liraglutide resulted in a significant improvement in their QoL. However, no differences were found in the risk for depression [84]. The SUSTAIN 6 was a 2-year, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with 3297 participants that showed improvement in HRQoL in patients who were treated with semaglutide [85]. The results of an analysis of overweight or obese people with comorbidities revealed that treatment with liraglutide is associated with better health-related quality of life after one year of therapy compared to a placebo, and that this effect is stable for long observation up to three years [86,87]. The analysis of data from 4725 participants across three randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trials that evaluated the efficacy and safety of liraglutide proved improvements in metabolic parameters and health-related quality of life.

Title: Effect of liraglutide on depressive symptoms in overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes: protocol for a pilot randomized controlled trial
Snippet: Introduction Patients with concurrent obesity, type 2 diabetes, and depression experience high disease severity and prevalence. This triad of conditions compromises quality of life and treatment adherence, further exacerbating disease progression. Therapeutic strategies for such patients must address both glycemic control and psychological well-being. Liraglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), offers benefits beyond glucose-lowering and weight reduction, with emerging evidence suggesting it may also alleviate depressive symptoms. Therefore, liraglutide represents a promising intervention for managing depression in patients with obesity and diabetes. Objectives This study aims to assess the therapeutic efficacy of liraglutide in overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes and comorbid depression, with a specific focus on its antidepressant effects. Methods This is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial. Sixty eligible participants will be randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either liraglutide (initiated at 0.6 mg/day, titrated weekly to a maximum of 1.8 mg/day) or a matched placebo, as an adjunct to standard care for 12 weeks. The primary endpoints include blood glucose levels, glycated hemoglobin, body mass index, Hamilton Depression Rating Scale score, and metrics derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (resting-state fMRI). Secondary endpoints will assess changes in inflammatory biomarkers (tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6), oxidative stress indicators (superoxide dismutase, malondialdehyde), homeostasis model assessment of insulin resistance, insulin sensitivity index, and homeostasis model assessment of β-cell function. Conclusions This trial will provide preliminary data on the effects of liraglutide on depressive symptoms in overweight/obese patients with type 2 diabetes. The findings are expected to provide a basis and reference for subsequent large-scale clinical research.

Title: Clinical Evidence of Antidepressant Effects of Insulin and Anti-Hyperglycemic Agents and Implications for the Pathophysiology of Depression—A Literature Review
Snippet: An open-label, short-term study with liraglutide reported significant reduction in depressive symptoms [33]. In this 4-week study, which included 19 subjects with MDD or bipolar disorder with impaired executive function, administration of liraglutide significantly reduced HDRS scores as a secondary outcome measure, as well as improving executive function. The change in HDRS score did not moderate the improvement in cognition. However, liraglutide failed to show a significant effect on depressive symptoms in an RCT [52]. Treatment with liraglutide for 26 weeks reduced body weight and HbA1c significantly more than standard therapy, but it reduced BDI scores by only one point, which was not significant when compared with the control group.

Title: Effect of liraglutide on depressive symptoms in overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes: protocol for a pilot randomized controlled trial
Snippet: Although recent meta-analyses support the efficacy of GLP-1RAs in improving depression scale scores (21), some studies suggest potential risks of inducing mood fluctuations or depressive symptoms (22).This inconsistency in evidence reflects the complexity of disease mechanisms and highlights the importance of conducting rigorous clinical studies. 

To this end, the project team designed a randomized, controlled, double-blind clinical trial: Effect of Liraglutide on Depressive Symptoms in Overweight or Obese Patients with Type 2 Diabetes: Protocol for a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial. The findings of this study will offer supportive evidence for liraglutide use in overweight or obese patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus comorbid with depression, and lay the groundwork for a definitive large-scale clinical study.

Title: Insights into a possible role of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in the treatment of depression
Snippet: In a small-scale four-week long, open-label study involving 14 individuals diagnosed with major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder, which also displayed impaired executive function, treatment with liraglutide significantly reduced Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) scores and improved executive function, however, at the same time it did not improve cognitive function in patients [122]. Conversely, in a randomized controlled trial involving adults with T2DM, administration of liraglutide for 26 weeks in addition to standard therapy with insulin, although significantly decreased body weight and levels of glycated hemoglobin HbA1c in patients, but at the same time failed to reduce Beck's Depression Inventory (BDI) scores (de Witt 2014). There are also few studies concerning the safety of GLP-1RA implementation in neuropsychiatric diseases. In a pooled analysis of phase 2 and 3a clinical trials of liraglutide for weight management, when administered once daily at a dose of 3.0 mg caused no major concerns regarding its neuropsychiatric safety [123].

Title: Metabolic Modulators in Depression: Emerging Molecular Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities
Snippet: The disruption of glycerophospholipid and sphingolipid metabolism may cause abnormal cell function in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and HP regions, leading to depression-like cognitive dysfunction [65]. Dulaglutide modulates key lipids such as sphingolipids, lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC), lysophosphatidylethanolamine (LPE), phosphatidylcholine (PC), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), and phosphatidylinositol (PI), which are all implicated in the pathological alterations associated with depressive disorder [66,67]. Increased PE and PC levels are closely linked to anxiety and depressive-like behaviors in individuals with MDD. LPC and LPE are significantly increased in MDD and show pronounced positive relationships with depression severity [68]. Dulaglutide, by restoring lipid balance, may potentially exert antidepressant effects [67]. N-acetyl-L-aspartic acid (NAA) is considered a marker of neuronal density and integrity in the brain, representing a primary metabolic pathway across various brain regions. Studies have shown that in rat models of CSDS and chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS), NAA levels are reduced in the amygdala (AMY) [69]. Dulaglutide may increase NAA levels in the hippocampus, indicating that it may be a potential therapeutic target for depressive disorder [67]. In the chronic mild stress model of depression (CMS), L-glutamic acid and L-arginine are upregulated. Dulaglutide decreased the levels of L-glutamic acid. attempts.answer:
Summary of the question and clinical context
GLP‑1 receptor agonists (RAs) are incretin therapies used for glycemic control and weight loss that increasingly show associations with mood outcomes. They have multiple putative mechanisms influencing mood, including central actions on brainstem, hypothalamic, and limbic circuits, modulation of monoamines/neuroinflammation, and systemic metabolic and reward-processing changes, alongside weight loss via reduced food intake and delayed gastric emptying. <cite id="463d4aba-3">Semaglutide crosses the blood–brain barrier and may modulate neuroinflammation and hippocampal plasticity, while liraglutide acts via neurotransmission modulation and neuronal survival, with central actions supported by preclinical and clinical data</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-2">Semaglutide and liraglutide reduce appetite, delay gastric emptying, and produce sustained weight loss over 52–68 weeks in large trials</cite> <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Semaglutide 2.4 mg maintained over 104 weeks produces similar average weight loss at 52 and 104 weeks, while weight regain occurs after discontinuation</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">FDA trials of semaglutide up to 68 weeks did not observe worsening of depression or suicidality among participants without severe psychiatric histories</cite>.

What outcomes indicate “antidepressant effects”?
Trials and observational studies use diverse endpoints. Clinical trials often measure depression scales (PHQ‑9, HADS, MADRS as in psychiatric subgroups), anhedonia, and overall mood/psychiatric diagnoses; pharmacovigilance and registry work examine incident depression, anxiety, suicidality, and psychiatric adverse events. <cite id="7a4b4581-1">A post hoc subgroup of the STEP trials assessed psychiatric medication use and noted that PHQ‑9 change was not analyzed centrally, with baseline PHQ‑9 ≥15 and current suicidality as exclusion criteria, but antidepressant use did not blunt semaglutide’s weight loss and may be countered by semaglutide’s appetite effects</cite> <cite id="da571204-1">A systematic review reports mixed findings: some studies show higher risk of anxiety/depression with GLP‑1 RAs, while others show reduced depression/anxiety scale scores and no increased anxiety among patients with T2D using GLP‑1 RAs</cite>.

1) Time course and onset of antidepressant/mood effects
Multiple pharmacovigilance analyses of large adverse‑event databases indicate that mood effects with GLP‑1 agonists tend to emerge within weeks of starting therapy. <cite id="463d4aba-0">Median times to onset of depressive disorders associated with liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide were 28.0 (3.5–40.0), 23.0 (1–69.0), and 31.0 (5.5–84.0) days, respectively</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-1">Semaglutide had a reporting odds ratio for depressive symptoms of 6.24 (95% CI 4.49–8.69) and 2.58 for suicidal ideation; liraglutide was linked to depression</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-4">Across US, Canada, and Australia, semaglutide and liraglutide showed significant associations with depression and suicidal ideation, with a large community cohort linking GLP‑1 RAs to a 108% increased risk of anxiety, 195% higher risk of major depression, and 106% elevated risk of suicidal behavior, primarily with liraglutide and semaglutide</cite>. These latency distributions imply that, in a subset of patients, mood changes can occur within approximately 4–8 weeks, with a long right tail to later onset.

Randomized and observational clinical evidence complements these timing inferences. <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">Case reports describe onset of depressive symptoms around 1 month after semaglutide initiation, with resolution after discontinuation</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">FDA review of semaglutide trials spanning 68 weeks did not observe worsening depression or suicidality in participants without prior severe psychiatric illness</cite> <cite id="da571204-1">A systematic review notes that while some cohorts show increased psychiatric risk with GLP‑1 RAs, others report lower depression/anxiety scale scores and no increased anxiety among T2D patients</cite>. Together, these data suggest antidepressant effects can emerge over weeks to a few months, but the balance and direction vary by population and study design, with some patients experiencing improvement and others worsening, particularly at higher doses or with psychiatric comorbidity.

2) Persistence of effects after weight stabilization
Trials show that with continued GLP‑1 dosing, weight and cardiometabolic outcomes can persist for up to 48–104 weeks; this provides a window during which mood effects may persist, contingent on ongoing pharmacologic exposure. <cite id="7a4b4581-0">In STEP 5, semaglutide 2.4 mg maintained for 52 and 104 weeks yielded similar average weight losses (−15.6% and −15.2%), whereas discontinuation led to weight regain in STEP 4 and STEP 1 off‑treatment extensions</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-0">STEP‑8 in adults with obesity without diabetes demonstrated greater weight loss over 68 weeks with semaglutide 2.4 mg than liraglutide 3 mg, supporting durable dosing and lifestyle support</cite> <cite id="7a4b4581-3">Semaglutide with lifestyle changes produced greater weight loss than liraglutide at 68 weeks, with structured maintenance and a 7‑week follow‑up</cite>. Within this dosing and follow‑up architecture, mood outcomes have been variably reported: <cite id="da571204-2">FDA trials did not document worsening depression or suicidality over 68 weeks among non‑high‑risk patients</cite>, while <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">case reports of semaglutide‑related depression improved after discontinuation</cite>. Mechanistic and trial‑adjacent evidence indicates two contributors to persistence: pharmacologic CNS occupancy and systemic metabolic/reward changes. <cite id="463d4aba-3">GLP‑1 analogs can cross the blood–brain barrier and modulate neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, and hippocampal plasticity, supporting potential long‑term mood actions with sustained dosing</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-2">Semaglutide reduces appetite and alters gastric emptying, producing durable weight loss that may stabilize over 52 weeks</cite>.

Importantly, weight loss itself is a mediator of mood improvement in obesity. Large lifestyle‑supported trials show that continued weight loss over months (e.g., 6–12 months) improves depressive symptoms and functioning in many patients with obesity, and weight stabilization is followed by plateau in these benefits unless dosing is maintained. <cite id="bcaa5c96-0">In STEP‑4, 803 participants who reached 2.4 mg/week semaglutide were randomized for 48 weeks of continued semaglutide or placebo, sustaining weight loss</cite> <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Average percent body weight loss remained stable at 52 and 104 weeks with maintained semaglutide dosing</cite>. Conversely, when weight loss plateaus or treatment stops, weight regain can reverse psychosocial and metabolic improvements, with some patients experiencing mood deterioration. <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Weight regain occurred after semaglutide discontinuation in STEP 4 and STEP 1 off‑treatment extensions</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">Depressive symptoms starting around 1 month on semaglutide resolved with discontinuation in case reports</cite>.

3) Magnitude, direction, and heterogeneity of effects
Findings across studies are mixed, reflecting differences in patient comorbidities, dosing regimens, and endpoints. <cite id="7a4b4581-1">Semaglutide reduced body weight versus placebo even in participants on psychotropics (antipsychotics/antidepressants), with similar outcomes to psychiatric comparators, suggesting pharmacologic appetite effects can counteract treatment‑induced increases in appetite for some psychiatric medications</cite> <cite id="da571204-1">A systematic review reports reduced depression/anxiety scale scores with GLP‑1 agonists in some trials, alongside observational cohorts showing increased risk of major depression and suicidal behavior, highlighting bidirectional relationships and heterogeneity across designs and populations</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-2">A systematic review concluded GLP‑1 agonists were significantly superior to controls for antidepressant symptomatology but emphasized unclear mechanisms and lack of causal evidence for depressive symptomatology</cite> <cite id="da571204-4">Reviews call the clinical evidence contradictory, with some trials supporting alleviation of depressive symptoms and others reporting exacerbation or suicidality attempts, and recommend larger, dual‑endpoint RCTs with HAM‑D and glycemic outcomes over ≥12 months</cite>. Notably, higher doses and prior psychiatric histories are risk factors for adverse mood outcomes, while continued dosing and integrated behavioral support mitigate weight regain and sustain psychosocial gains. <cite id="da571204-0">Higher semaglutide doses (e.g., 2.4 mg) were associated with higher psychiatric event incidence in observational data, and trials showed increased psychiatric event rates with higher semaglutide doses</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">Patients with no prior severe psychiatric history did not show worsening depression or suicidality in FDA‑reviewed semaglutide trials</cite>.

4) Practical implications for treatment duration and follow-up
- Onset: Antidepressant/mood effects can emerge within weeks to a few months of starting GLP‑1 therapy, with a typical latency of roughly 23–28 days in pharmacovigilance databases; clinicians may begin to see mood/anhedonia changes by 8–12 weeks, with continued monitoring thereafter. <cite id="463d4aba-0">Median times to onset of depressive disorders with liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide were 28, 23, and 31 days, respectively</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">No worsening of depression or suicidality was observed over 68 weeks in FDA trials, suggesting that sustained dosing can be followed without deterioration in low‑risk patients</cite>.
- Persistence after stabilization: Mood benefits tend to track weight loss trajectories—improving with ongoing weight loss and stabilizing or persisting with continued GLP‑1 dosing; discontinuation or dose reduction can precipitate weight regain and, in some patients, mood relapse. <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Average weight loss stabilized at 52 and 104 weeks with maintained semaglutide; discontinuation led to weight regain</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">Depressive symptoms emerging ~1 month after semaglutide improved after discontinuation in case reports</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-2">Semaglutide’s effects on appetite and gastric emptying underlie durable weight loss over 52 weeks</cite>.
- Dosing strategy: To maximize persistence of mood benefits after weight stabilization, many clinicians favor continuing GLP‑1 maintenance doses with structured lifestyle support rather than abrupt cessation. <cite id="bcaa5c96-0">Sustained weight loss over 48 additional weeks was achieved with continued semaglutide 2.4 mg</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-1">Semaglutide outperformed liraglutide for weight loss and cardiometabolic risk over 68 weeks, supporting long‑term maintenance strategies</cite>.
- Risk stratification: Patients with prior depression, suicidality, or anxiety may require baseline psychiatric evaluation, careful monitoring in the first 8–12 weeks, and consideration of lower effective doses with gradual titration. <cite id="da571204-0">Patients with psychiatric histories had higher psychiatric event rates with semaglutide; higher doses (2.4 mg) were associated with more psychiatric events in observational data</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">FDA trials did not show worsening in non‑high‑risk patients, but screening is recommended for those at risk</cite>.

Snippet: Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) analogues are a class of medications that stimulate glucose-dependent insulin release and slow gastric emptying. With the increasing use of GLP-1 analogues, concerns about potential psychiatric adverse events (AEs) remain under-explored. This pharmacovigilance study aimed to investigate the prevalence of psychiatric AEs associated with currently available GLP-1 analogues by analysing publicly available national datasets from the US (FAERS), Canada (CVAROD) and Australia (DAEN). Psychiatric AE reports were extracted from all three databases for all approved GLP-1 analogues. Title: Psychiatric effects of GLP‐1 receptor agonists: A systematic review of emerging evidence
Snippet: Beyond their metabolic effects, GLP-1RAs have been investigated for their potential impact on anxiety disorders, including GAD. Findings to date are mixed, with some studies suggesting anxiolytic effects and others raising concerns about possible adverse outcomes. 

A large-scale observational study using data from over 11 million adults with obesity found that GLP-1RA users had a significantly increased risk of developing psychiatric conditions compared to nonusers. Specifically, GLP-1RA users demonstrated a 108% increased risk of anxiety disorders, a 195% higher risk of major depressive disorder and a 106% increased risk of suicidal behaviour. 13 These associations remained consistent across demographic subgroups and specific GLP-1RAs, including semaglutide and liraglutide. Similarly, a pharmacovigilance analysis of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) identified a statistically significant association between GLP-1RAs and reported psychiatric adverse events. 31 Anxiety, nervousness and insomnia were among the most frequently reported psychiatric adverse events, with a small increase in reporting frequency (ROR = 1.04). 31  contrast, several studies suggest that GLP-1RAs may confer some protective effects against anxiety. A population-based cohort study reported a lower risk of anxiety among individuals with T2DM treated with GLP-1RAs compared to non-users. 32 These findings were supported by a meta-analysis demonstrating significant reductions in depression and anxiety scale scores among GLP-1RA users compared to controls. 11 Additionally, a study of semaglutide use in individuals with T2DM found no increased risk of anxiety or depression and reported a lower risk of cognitive impairment. 33 ese contradictory findings underscore the complex and potentially bidirectional relationship between GLP-1RAs and psychiatric outcomes. Heterogeneity in study design, patient populations and specific GLP-1RAs examined likely contributes to these inconsistencies. Further large-scale, prospective studies are needed to elucidate the psychiatric risk-benefit profile of GLP-1RAs across diverse clinical populations.

Summary of the question and clinical context
GLP‑1 receptor agonists (RAs) are incretin therapies used for glycemic control and weight loss that increasingly show associations with mood outcomes. They have multiple putative mechanisms influencing mood, including central actions on brainstem, hypothalamic, and limbic circuits, modulation of monoamines/neuroinflammation, and systemic metabolic and reward-processing changes, alongside weight loss via reduced food intake and delayed gastric emptying. <cite id="463d4aba-3">Semaglutide crosses the blood–brain barrier and may modulate neuroinflammation and hippocampal plasticity, while liraglutide acts via neurotransmission modulation and neuronal survival, with central actions supported by preclinical and clinical data</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-2">Semaglutide and liraglutide reduce appetite, delay gastric emptying, and produce sustained weight loss over 52–68 weeks in large trials</cite> <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Semaglutide 2.4 mg maintained over 104 weeks produces similar average weight loss at 52 and 104 weeks, while weight regain occurs after discontinuation</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">FDA trials of semaglutide up to 68 weeks did not observe worsening of depression or suicidality among participants without severe psychiatric histories</cite>.

What outcomes indicate “antidepressant effects”?
Trials and observational studies use diverse endpoints. Clinical trials often measure depression scales (PHQ‑9, HADS, MADRS as in psychiatric subgroups), anhedonia, and overall mood/psychiatric diagnoses; pharmacovigilance and registry work examine incident depression, anxiety, suicidality, and psychiatric adverse events. <cite id="7a4b4581-1">A post hoc subgroup of the STEP trials assessed psychiatric medication use and noted that PHQ‑9 change was not analyzed centrally, with baseline PHQ‑9 ≥15 and current suicidality as exclusion criteria, but antidepressant use did not blunt semaglutide’s weight loss and may be countered by semaglutide’s appetite effects</cite> <cite id="da571204-1">A systematic review reports mixed findings: some studies show higher risk of anxiety/depression with GLP‑1 RAs, while others show reduced depression/anxiety scale scores and no increased anxiety among patients with T2D using GLP‑1 RAs</cite>.

1) Time course and onset of antidepressant/mood effects
Multiple pharmacovigilance analyses of large adverse‑event databases indicate that mood effects with GLP‑1 agonists tend to emerge within weeks of starting therapy. <cite id="463d4aba-0">Median times to onset of depressive disorders associated with liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide were 28.0 (3.5–40.0), 23.0 (1–69.0), and 31.0 (5.5–84.0) days, respectively</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-1">Semaglutide had a reporting odds ratio for depressive symptoms of 6.24 (95% CI 4.49–8.69) and 2.58 for suicidal ideation; liraglutide was linked to depression</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-4">Across US, Canada, and Australia, semaglutide and liraglutide showed significant associations with depression and suicidal ideation, with a large community cohort linking GLP‑1 RAs to a 108% increased risk of anxiety, 195% higher risk of major depression, and 106% elevated risk of suicidal behavior, primarily with liraglutide and semaglutide</cite>. These latency distributions imply that, in a subset of patients, mood changes can occur within approximately 4–8 weeks, with a long right tail to later onset.

Randomized and observational clinical evidence complements these timing inferences. <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">Case reports describe onset of depressive symptoms around 1 month after semaglutide initiation, with resolution after discontinuation</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">FDA review of semaglutide trials spanning 68 weeks did not observe worsening depression or suicidality in participants without prior severe psychiatric illness</cite> <cite id="da571204-1">A systematic review notes that while some cohorts show increased psychiatric risk with GLP‑1 RAs, others report lower depression/anxiety scale scores and no increased anxiety among T2D patients</cite>. Together, these data suggest antidepressant effects can emerge over weeks to a few months, but the balance and direction vary by population and study design, with some patients experiencing improvement and others worsening, particularly at higher doses or with psychiatric comorbidity.

2) Persistence of effects after weight stabilization
Trials show that with continued GLP‑1 dosing, weight and cardiometabolic outcomes can persist for up to 48–104 weeks; this provides a window during which mood effects may persist, contingent on ongoing pharmacologic exposure. <cite id="7a4b4581-0">In STEP 5, semaglutide 2.4 mg maintained for 52 and 104 weeks yielded similar average weight losses (−15.6% and −15.2%), whereas discontinuation led to weight regain in STEP 4 and STEP 1 off‑treatment extensions</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-0">STEP‑8 in adults with obesity without diabetes demonstrated greater weight loss over 68 weeks with semaglutide 2.4 mg than liraglutide 3 mg, supporting durable dosing and lifestyle support</cite> <cite id="7a4b4581-3">Semaglutide with lifestyle changes produced greater weight loss than liraglutide at 68 weeks, with structured maintenance and a 7‑week follow‑up</cite>. Within this dosing and follow‑up architecture, mood outcomes have been variably reported: <cite id="da571204-2">FDA trials did not document worsening depression or suicidality over 68 weeks among non‑high‑risk patients</cite>, while <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">case reports of semaglutide‑related depression improved after discontinuation</cite>. Mechanistic and trial‑adjacent evidence indicates two contributors to persistence: pharmacologic CNS occupancy and systemic metabolic/reward changes. <cite id="463d4aba-3">GLP‑1 analogs can cross the blood–brain barrier and modulate neurotransmission, neuroinflammation, and hippocampal plasticity, supporting potential long‑term mood actions with sustained dosing</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-2">Semaglutide reduces appetite and alters gastric emptying, producing durable weight loss that may stabilize over 52 weeks</cite>.

Importantly, weight loss itself is a mediator of mood improvement in obesity. Large lifestyle‑supported trials show that continued weight loss over months (e.g., 6–12 months) improves depressive symptoms and functioning in many patients with obesity, and weight stabilization is followed by plateau in these benefits unless dosing is maintained. <cite id="bcaa5c96-0">In STEP‑4, 803 participants who reached 2.4 mg/week semaglutide were randomized for 48 weeks of continued semaglutide or placebo, sustaining weight loss</cite> <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Average percent body weight loss remained stable at 52 and 104 weeks with maintained semaglutide dosing</cite>. Conversely, when weight loss plateaus or treatment stops, weight regain can reverse psychosocial and metabolic improvements, with some patients experiencing mood deterioration. <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Weight regain occurred after semaglutide discontinuation in STEP 4 and STEP 1 off‑treatment extensions</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">Depressive symptoms starting around 1 month on semaglutide resolved with discontinuation in case reports</cite>.

3) Magnitude, direction, and heterogeneity of effects
Findings across studies are mixed, reflecting differences in patient comorbidities, dosing regimens, and endpoints. <cite id="7a4b4581-1">Semaglutide reduced body weight versus placebo even in participants on psychotropics (antipsychotics/antidepressants), with similar outcomes to psychiatric comparators, suggesting pharmacologic appetite effects can counteract treatment‑induced increases in appetite for some psychiatric medications</cite> <cite id="da571204-1">A systematic review reports reduced depression/anxiety scale scores with GLP‑1 agonists in some trials, alongside observational cohorts showing increased risk of major depression and suicidal behavior, highlighting bidirectional relationships and heterogeneity across designs and populations</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-2">A systematic review concluded GLP‑1 agonists were significantly superior to controls for antidepressant symptomatology but emphasized unclear mechanisms and lack of causal evidence for depressive symptomatology</cite> <cite id="da571204-4">Reviews call the clinical evidence contradictory, with some trials supporting alleviation of depressive symptoms and others reporting exacerbation or suicidality attempts, and recommend larger, dual‑endpoint RCTs with HAM‑D and glycemic outcomes over ≥12 months</cite>. Notably, higher doses and prior psychiatric histories are risk factors for adverse mood outcomes, while continued dosing and integrated behavioral support mitigate weight regain and sustain psychosocial gains. <cite id="da571204-0">Higher semaglutide doses (e.g., 2.4 mg) were associated with higher psychiatric event incidence in observational data, and trials showed increased psychiatric event rates with higher semaglutide doses</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">Patients with no prior severe psychiatric history did not show worsening depression or suicidality in FDA‑reviewed semaglutide trials</cite>.

4) Practical implications for treatment duration and follow-up
- Onset: Antidepressant/mood effects can emerge within weeks to a few months of starting GLP‑1 therapy, with a typical latency of roughly 23–28 days in pharmacovigilance databases; clinicians may begin to see mood/anhedonia changes by 8–12 weeks, with continued monitoring thereafter. <cite id="463d4aba-0">Median times to onset of depressive disorders with liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide were 28, 23, and 31 days, respectively</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">No worsening of depression or suicidality was observed over 68 weeks in FDA trials, suggesting that sustained dosing can be followed without deterioration in low‑risk patients</cite>.
- Persistence after stabilization: Mood benefits tend to track weight loss trajectories—improving with ongoing weight loss and stabilizing or persisting with continued GLP‑1 dosing; discontinuation or dose reduction can precipitate weight regain and, in some patients, mood relapse. <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Average weight loss stabilized at 52 and 104 weeks with maintained semaglutide; discontinuation led to weight regain</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">Depressive symptoms emerging ~1 month after semaglutide improved after discontinuation in case reports</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-2">Semaglutide’s effects on appetite and gastric emptying underlie durable weight loss over 52 weeks</cite>.
- Dosing strategy: To maximize persistence of mood benefits after weight stabilization, many clinicians favor continuing GLP‑1 maintenance doses with structured lifestyle support rather than abrupt cessation. <cite id="bcaa5c96-0">Sustained weight loss over 48 additional weeks was achieved with continued semaglutide 2.4 mg</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-1">Semaglutide outperformed liraglutide for weight loss and cardiometabolic risk over 68 weeks, supporting long‑term maintenance strategies</cite>.
- Risk stratification: Patients with prior depression, suicidality, or anxiety may require baseline psychiatric evaluation, careful monitoring in the first 8–12 weeks, and consideration of lower effective doses with gradual titration. <cite id="da571204-0">Patients with psychiatric histories had higher psychiatric event rates with semaglutide; higher doses (2.4 mg) were associated with more psychiatric events in observational data</cite> <cite id="da571204-2">FDA trials did not show worsening in non‑high‑risk patients, but screening is recommended for those at risk</cite>.

5) What remains uncertain
Key gaps include standardized, disease‑modifying endpoints for mood (e.g., MADRS, HAM‑D alongside weight) over multi‑year horizons and head‑to‑head comparisons of agents and dosing on depressive symptoms independent of weight. <cite id="da571204-4">A multicenter, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled RCT with dual HAM‑D and glycemic endpoints over ≥12 months is warranted; current evidence is contradictory and lacks dose‑dependency and subgroup comparisons</cite>. Additionally, the degree to which weight‑independent CNS effects explain observed benefits vs. the contribution of sustained weight loss remains under study. <cite id="463d4aba-2">Studies indicate antidepressant symptomatology benefits versus controls but mechanisms are unclear</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-3">Preliminary data suggest central neuroprotective and neuroplastic mechanisms for semaglutide</cite>.

Practical answer to the question
- Treatment duration to emerge: Antidepressant/mood effects with GLP‑1 agonists can emerge within weeks of initiation, commonly between 4 and 12 weeks, with pharmacovigilance analyses showing median time‑to‑onset of 23–28 days for depressive events and case reports of symptom onset around 1 month; sustained dosing over months (e.g., 6–12+ months) is typically needed to consolidate benefits, and structured lifestyle support improves durability. <cite id="463d4aba-0">Median times to onset of depressive disorders with liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide were 28, 23, and 31 days, respectively</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">Depressive symptoms starting ~1 month after semaglutide improved after discontinuation</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-0">Sustained weight loss over 48 additional weeks was achieved with continued semaglutide 2.4 mg</cite>.
- Persistence after weight stabilization: In many patients, mood benefits stabilize alongside weight as they plateau and can persist with continued GLP‑1 dosing; discontinuation or dose reduction often precipitates weight regain and, in a subset, mood relapse. However, effects are heterogeneous—some patients improve and maintain mood benefits independent of weight via central mechanisms, while others see improvements largely tied to ongoing weight loss. <cite id="7a4b4581-0">Average percent body weight loss remained stable at 52 and 104 weeks with maintained semaglutide, while discontinuation led to weight regain</cite> <cite id="bcaa5c96-3">Depressive symptoms emerging around 1 month improved after semaglutide discontinuation</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-3">GLP‑1 analogs may exert antidepressant effects via central neuroinflammation and hippocampal plasticity</cite> <cite id="463d4aba-4">Large cohorts show higher risks of major depression and suicidal behavior with GLP‑1 RAs, underscoring heterogeneity</cite>.

Title: Psychiatric adverse events linked to glucagon-like peptide 1 analogues: a disproportionality analysis in American, Canadian and Australian adverse event databases
Snippet: Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) analogues are a class of medications that stimulate glucose-dependent insulin release and slow gastric emptying. With the increasing use of GLP-1 analogues, concerns about potential psychiatric adverse events (AEs) remain under-explored. This pharmacovigilance study aimed to investigate the prevalence of psychiatric AEs associated with currently available GLP-1 analogues by analysing publicly available national datasets from the US (FAERS), Canada (CVAROD) and Australia (DAEN). Psychiatric AE reports were extracted from all three databases for all approved GLP-1 analogues. A disproportionality analysis was conducted to calculate reporting odds ratios (RORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for psychiatric AEs of interest. Significant associations were identified when multiple databases reported elevated RORs. Semaglutide was associated with depressive symptoms (FAERS, ROR = 6.24 CI 4.49–8.69), panic attacks (FAERS, ROR = 1.46 CI 1.16–1.82) and suicidal ideation (FAERS, ROR = 2.58 CI 2.31–2.88). Liraglutide was linked to depression (CVAROD, ROR = 1.68 CI 1.12–2.51), while dulaglutide showed positive associations with eating disorders (FAERS, ROR = 1.47 CI 1.26–1.71) and insomnia (FAERS, ROR = 2.93 CI 2.35–3.66). GLP-1 analogues, particularly semaglutide and liraglutide, are associated with significant psychiatric AEs, especially depression and suicidal ideation. Further studies are required to understand the mechanisms underlying these associations, particularly in patients with pre-existing psychiatric conditions.

Title: Causal relationship between GLP-1 agonists and depressive symptomatology in patients with type 2 Diabetes: A systematic review
Snippet: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists are drugs used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and some (Liraglutide and Semaglutide) for weight loss with significant effects on visceral fat. Adverse effects include gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting or diarrhea and is associated with an increased frequency of acute pancreatitis. Material and methods: This systematic review has used search engines such as PubMed, Google Scholar, Cochrane and the Acsess Medicine platform to search for literature investigating the effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists versus other antidiabetic therapies on depressive symptoms including suicidal ideation, finding a total of 07 potential articles related to the use of GLP-1 agonists and their neuropsychological effects. Results: Of the 7 articles analyzed, the type of study design, the period, the number of patients included, the number of patients diagnosed with diabetes, and the use of GLP-1 agonist versus other control treatment therapies are detailed. Conclusion: The studies reviewed indicate that GLP-1 agonists were significantly superior to control treatments in relation to the effect of antidepressant symptomatology, the mechanism by which this effect occurs remains unclear. We found no available verifiable evidence showing a causal association of GLP-1 agonists and depressive symptomatology in patients with type 2 Diabetes.

Title: Optimizing obesity management for women in an Indian obstetrics and gynecology setting: A consensus approach by the Indian Society of Assisted Reproduction (ISAR)
Snippet: obust mean weight loss in the range of 13-18% was reported in STEP trials (Semaglutide Treatment Effect in People with Obesity) with injectable semaglutide 2.4 mg. The STEP 4 Randomized Clinical Trial inspected the impact of current weekly subcutaneous Semaglutide versus placebo on the maintenance of weight loss in adults with obesity. The study aimed to determine whether Semaglutide could help sustain weight loss in this population. The STEP-4 trial, a total of 902 individuals received onceweekly subcutaneous semaglutide. After 20 weeks (16 weeks of dose escalation; 4 weeks of maintenance dose), 803 participants (89.0%) who had reached the 2.4-mg/week semaglutide maintenance dose were randomised (2:1) to 48 weeks of continued subcutaneous semaglutide (n = 535) or placebo (n = 268), with lifestyle intervention in both groups. STEP-4 trial established that among adults with obesity, subcutaneous semaglutide (2.4 mg) once weekly enabled continued weight loss over 48 weeks. 47 Similarly, the STEP-8 trial reported that among adults with obesity without diabetes, once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg along with counselling for diet and physical activity enabled substantially greater weight loss at 68 weeks compared to once-daily subcutaneous liraglutide 3 mg. 48 eight loss due to semaglutide seems to be due to improved appetite control, and subsequent decreased energy intake, through effects in the hypothalamus and area postrema of the brain. 47 A few RCTs showed similar significant weight loss outcomes with semaglutide. 50,51 The major side effects seen with semaglutide were gastrointestinal tract disorders. However, most gastrointestinal events were transient and mild-to-moderate in severity, and most patients recovered without treatment discontinuation. 47

Title: Obesity: Genetic Insights, Therapeutic Strategies, Pharmacoeconomic Impact, and Psychosocial Dimensions
Snippet: Liraglutide shares the same mechanism of action as semaglutide but is less potent, requires daily administration, and achieves comparatively lower weight loss outcomes [64]. In the SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes trial (n = 3731), liraglutide 3 mg plus lifestyle changes led to greater weight loss (−8.4 ± 7.3 kg) than placebo (−2.8 ± 6.5 kg; p < 0.001) after 56 weeks [66]. Additionally, when comparing in a randomized clinical trial once-weekly semaglutide with once-daily liraglutide in adults with overweight or obesity (without diabetes), we found that semaglutide was more effective in reducing body weight. At 68 weeks, semaglutide resulted in significantly greater weight loss, with a higher proportion of participants achieving clinically meaningful reductions of 5-15%, as well as greater improvements in several cardiometabolic risk factors [53]. Both agents promote weight loss primarily through decreased energy intake; however, the effect was more pronounced with semaglutide compared with liraglutide (around 16%) [67]. 

Adverse events were predominantly gastrointestinal in both drugs, though treatment discontinuation rates were higher with liraglutide, likely due to its shorter half-life, more frequent dosing, and dose-escalation tolerability issues. These findings align with prior evidence from the STEP 1 (semaglutide) and SCALE (liraglutide) trials [68].

Title: Long-Term Efficacy and Safety of Anti-Obesity Treatment: Where Do We Stand?
Snippet: Semaglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 analog that can be administered once a week, while liraglutide is a short-acting GLP-1 analog that should be administered daily. Semaglutide, similar to liraglutide, was recently approved in Europe, Japan, and North America as a treatment for T2DM. Semaglutide not only regulates blood sugar similar to native GLP-1 but also plays a role in reducing energy intake, increasing satiety, and reducing hunger. In a previous study, administration of 1 mg of semaglutide once every week for 12 weeks resulted in a weight loss of 5 kg, decreased appetite and food cravings, better controlled diet, and reduced preference for fatty or energy-rich foods [65]. In another study conducted by the same research team, a 12-week semaglutide, placebo crossover test was conducted in 30 obese patients. In the group administered with semaglutide once a week (with gradual escalation to 1 mg per week), both glucose and lipid metabolism (fasting and after meals) as well as the first-hour gastric emptying time was delayed [66]. In addition, a phase 2 clinical study, conducted for 52 weeks, revealed the long-term effects of semaglutide on weight loss in adults with obesity. One is a middle-aged man with no previous history of depression who developed depressive symptoms about 1 month after taking semaglutide. Depression was improved or relieved after discontinuation of semaglutide in both cases. On June 1, 2023, a 54-year-old man came to Peking Union Medical College Hospital (Beijing, China) with a complaint of decreased energy and motivation for more than 1 month. Liraglutide shares the same mechanism of action as semaglutide but is less potent, requires daily administration, and achieves comparatively lower weight loss outcomes [64]. In the SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes trial (n = 3731), liraglutide 3 mg plus lifestyle changes led to greater weight loss (−8.4 ± 7.3 kg) than placebo (−2.8 ± 6.5 kg; p < 0.001) after 56 weeks [66]. At 68 weeks, semaglutide resulted in significantly greater weight loss, with a higher proportion of participants achieving clinically meaningful reductions of 5-15%, as well as greater improvements in several cardiometabolic risk factors [53]. Adverse events were predominantly gastrointestinal in both drugs, though treatment discontinuation rates were higher with liraglutide, likely due to its shorter half-life, more frequent dosing, and dose-escalation tolerability issues. Semaglutide, similar to liraglutide, was recently approved in Europe, Japan, and North America as a treatment for T2DM. Title: Efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg for weight loss in overweight or obese adults without diabetes: An updated systematic review and meta‐analysis including the 2‐year STEP 5 trial
Snippet: To the best of our knowledge, it is typical for individuals to regain weight after initially losing it through behavioural 33,34 and other pharmacological interventions. 35,36In contrast to these findings, the longest trial lasting 2 years, referred to as STEP 5, showed that treatment with semaglutide 2.4 mg resulted in similar average weight loss at weeks 52 and 104 (À15.6% and À15.2%, respectively). 19These findings indicate that, on average, there is in BW over 104 weeks when the once-weekly semaglutide dose is continued.In addition, weight regain was observed following the discontinuation of semaglutide in both the STEP 4 withdrawal trial (after 20 weeks of treatment) and the STEP 1 off-treatment extension study (after 68 weeks of treatment). 18,37The aforementioned findings, along with the outcomes of our subgroup analysis considering various treatment durations, consistently affirm the substantial advantages of maintaining treatment with semaglutide for sustained weight loss.Additionally, in each of the included STEP trials, a lifestyle intervention was employed; however, only the STEP 3 trial incorporated high-intensity behavioural therapy and an initial low-calorie meal-substitution regimen.Nevertheless, we note that the semaglutide groups demonstrated a significant reduction in weight at the end of the treatment period for various steps, namely, 14.9% for STEP 1, 16% for STEP 3, 17.4% for STEP 4, 15.2% for STEP 5, and 15.8% for STEP 8. [16][17][18][19][20] This raises a new question of whether some lifestyle adjustments are needed for the efficacy of semaglutide 2.4 mg, thus, further clinical trials are needed to address this issue in the future.

The effects of semaglutide on the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) are postulated to mediate weight loss by influencing various brain regions, such as the hypothalamus, hindbrain, and lateral parabrachial nucleus.

Title: Efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg according to antidepressant use at baseline: A post hoc subgroup analysis
Snippet: Despite participants with psychiatric disorders also receiving antipsychotic drugs and ADs, the weight loss achieved was generally similar to that of their counterparts [23].Although participants in our study were categorized according to AD medication use at baseline, and participants in the liraglutide study were grouped according to whether they had psychiatric disorders, by comparison, the findings with liraglutide support our results, with participants on ADs achieving equal if not greater weight loss than those not on ADs at baseline.

Similar to the findings of the current study, the most common side effects with liraglutide were gastrointestinal, and the prevalence of these events was relatively low.Additionally, rates of discontinuation of liraglutide were higher in participants with psychiatric disorders versus those without [23].

Increased appetite has been reported by some individuals (albeit not all) taking ADs [9].The observed reductions in body weight with semaglutide versus placebo in participants on ADs at baseline (compared with those who were not) suggests that semaglutide could potentially counteract the increased appetite caused by some ADs.

Further study of this issue is needed.

The current analysis had several limitations: first, its post hoc nature means the results should be interpreted with caution.Due to T A B L E 3 Proportion of participants with adverse events across the STEP 1-3 and 5 trials in participants with and without AD use at baseline data availability, history of psychiatric disorders, diagnosed depression/mood disorders, or diagnosed anxiety was used to gauge the clinical context of the population in both groups, rather than assessing baseline psychiatric conditions.A significant proportion of participants may have been prescribed ADs for conditions other than depression, such as anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, sleep disturbance, pain, and neuropathy, which have accounted for up to 50% of prescriptions in some surveys [12,13]; therefore, AD use in this population may not signify depression.The change from baseline in PHQ-9

scores was not analyzed, and the study did not assess the impact of semaglutide on symptoms of depression.Patients with a PHQ-9 score ≥15 were excluded from the trial, as were those with a history of a suicide attempt or current suicidal ideation.

Title: The Impact Once-Weekly Semaglutide 2.4 mg Will Have on Clinical Practice: A Focus on the STEP Trials
Snippet: The STEP 8 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04074161) was an open label with treatment arms and double-blinded against matched placebo arms [28]. It included adults with the same inclusion and exclusion criteria as the STEP 1 trial. In a 3:1:3:1 ratio, the trial randomized 338 participants to either once-weekly semaglutide (dose-escalation to 2.4 mg over 16 weeks), or matching placebo, or once-daily liraglutide (dose escalation to 3.0 mg over 4 weeks), or matching placebo. Both semaglutide and liraglutide are long-acting GLP-1 analogs. As a result of the substitution of amino acids that prevents the degeneration of dipeptidyl peptidase 4 and addition of C18 fatty acids, semaglutide has a half-life of 165 h, whereas liraglutide's half-life is about 13 h [26]. All the participants in this trial had the same lifestyle intervention as the STEP 1 trial. The study continued for 75 weeks; the treatments lasted for 68 weeks, trailed by a 7-week follow-up period with no medications. The mean age and BMI of participants were 49 years and 37.5 kg/m 2 , respectively. The majority of the research participants were females (78.4%) and of White ethnicity (73.7%). 

Semaglutide with lifestyle modifications resulted in a more significant weight loss from baseline to week 68 compared to liraglutide with lifestyle modifications (MD = −9.4%, 95% CI: −12.0, −6.8). Furthermore, the proportions of the semaglutide patients who achieved ≥5%, ≥10%, ≥15%, and ≥20% body weight loss at week 68 were 87.2%, 70.9%, 55.6%, and 38.5%, respectively.

Liraglutide shares the same mechanism of action as semaglutide but is less potent, requires daily administration, and achieves comparatively lower weight loss outcomes [64]. In the SCALE Obesity and Prediabetes trial (n = 3731), liraglutide 3 mg plus lifestyle changes led to greater weight loss (−8.4 ± 7.3 kg) than placebo (−2.8 ± 6.5 kg; p < 0.001) after 56 weeks [66]. Additionally, when comparing in a randomized clinical trial once-weekly semaglutide with once-daily liraglutide in adults with overweight or obesity (without diabetes), we found that semaglutide was more effective in reducing body weight. At 68 weeks, semaglutide resulted in significantly greater weight loss, with a higher proportion of participants achieving clinically meaningful reductions of 5-15%, as well as greater improvements in several cardiometabolic risk factors [53]. Both agents promote weight loss primarily through decreased energy intake; however, the effect was more pronounced with semaglutide compared with liraglutide (around 16%) [67]. 

Adverse events were predominantly gastrointestinal in both drugs, though treatment discontinuation rates were higher with liraglutide, likely due to its shorter half-life, more frequent dosing, and dose-escalation tolerability issues. The STEP 8 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04074161) was an open label with treatment arms and double-blinded against matched placebo arms [28]. It included adults with the same inclusion and exclusion criteria as the STEP 1 trial. In a 3:1:3:1 ratio, the trial randomized 338 participants to either once-weekly semaglutide (dose-escalation to 2.4 mg over 16 weeks), or matching placebo, or once-daily liraglutide (dose escalation to 3.0 mg over 4 weeks), or matching placebo. Both semaglutide and liraglutide are long-acting GLP-1 analogs. As a result of the substitution of amino acids that prevents the degeneration of dipeptidyl peptidase 4 and addition of C18 fatty acids, semaglutide has a half-life of 165 h, whereas liraglutide's half-life is about 13 h [26]. All the participants in this trial had the same lifestyle intervention as the STEP 1 trial. The study continued for 75 weeks; the treatments lasted for 68 weeks, trailed by a 7-week follow-up period with no medications. The mean age and BMI of participants were 49 years and 37.5 kg/m 2 , respectively. The majority of the research participants were females (78.4%) and of White ethnicity (73.7%). 

Semaglutide with lifestyle modifications resulted in a more significant weight loss from baseline to week 68 compared to liraglutide with lifestyle modifications (MD = −9.4%, 95% CI: −12.0, −6.8). Furthermore, the proportions of the semaglutide patients who achieved ≥5%, ≥10%, ≥15%, and ≥20% body weight loss at week 68 were 87.2%, 70.9%, 55.6%, and 38.5%, respectively.

The STEP 4 Randomized Clinical Trial inspected the impact of current weekly subcutaneous Semaglutide versus placebo on the maintenance of weight loss in adults with obesity. The study aimed to determine whether Semaglutide could help sustain weight loss in this population. The STEP-4 trial, a total of 902 individuals received onceweekly subcutaneous semaglutide. After 20 weeks (16 weeks of dose escalation; 4 weeks of maintenance dose), 803 participants (89.0%) who had reached the 2.4-mg/week semaglutide maintenance dose were randomised (2:1) to 48 weeks of continued subcutaneous semaglutide (n = 535) or placebo (n = 268), with lifestyle intervention in both groups. However, most gastrointestinal events were transient and mild-to-moderate in severity, and most patients recovered without treatment discontinuation. 47
